Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00549

There is also a fourth use: whether something will be affirmed or denied in the future. This is called “future possibility.” Whatever belongs to the past or present has either happened or not happened, so it has already been placed at one end of the scale by necessity. Some logicians therefore held that only future things whose outcome is unknown remain purely possible. Some insist that a future possibility must not yet exist. They overlook a difficulty with their own test. If supposing the thing already exists makes its existence necessary, then supposing that it does not yet exist also makes its present nonexistence necessary. If the first supposition destroys possibility, why would the second not do so too? Neither deserves preference. This view suits the methods of logic and discursive argument.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00550

But a closer philosophical inquiry gives a different answer. Even a future event does not escape necessity. Given its causes, one outcome must occur and its opposite cannot occur, just as with events in the present. What it means for a thing to be possible therefore does not change when we look from the present to the future. The difference is that, with a future event, we do not yet know which side will prove true. For something in the past or present has already happened or failed to happen, and a statement about it is true or false according to whether it matches what occurred. With a future event, we are still asking which outcome will become real.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00551

This uncertainty belongs to our knowledge, which does not encompass all that has happened and all that will happen. The knowledge of the first principles and sources of existence, by contrast, encompasses events fully. It is all-encompassing and certain, not receptive, tentative, or doubtful. Possibility and uncertainty concern an essence that, by itself, calls for neither existence nor nonexistence. But this does not mean that the outcome is uncertain in reality. A thing is possible in itself, necessary when its cause exists, and impossible when its cause is absent. Most people think the future remains unsettled in reality, but careful inquiry rules that out.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00552

If all we know about a possible thing is that it is possible, we cannot tell whether it will exist. If we know that its cause exists, then its existence is necessary; if we know that its cause is absent, its nonexistence is necessary. In relation to their causes, then, possible things are necessary. If we knew every cause of one thing and knew that they were all present, we could be certain that the thing would exist: the presence of its causes would make it necessary.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00553

God knows future events through their causes. Those causes ultimately lead back to the Necessary Being. Every event that is possible in itself is necessary through its cause; if its cause did not make it necessary, the event would not occur. Its cause, too, is made necessary by another cause, until we reach the source of all causes, which has no cause. Because God knows how the causes are ordered, He knows events without any trace of doubt.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00554

An astrologer, by contrast, looks into only some of the causes. A prediction based on them remains a guess, however plausible, because an unseen obstacle may prevent the expected result. The causes observed are not yet the full cause unless everything that could block them has also been ruled out. As more causes become known, the prediction gains strength. With knowledge of all the causes, it becomes certain. For example, in winter we can know that the air will grow hot six months later because the sun will pass close to the point overhead. In the northern regions, this happens when the sun is in the northern signs of the zodiac. From the positions of the heavens and God’s unchanging order, one can know that the sun’s course will not change and that it will return to Leo after this interval. I will explain this more fully later, when I discuss how God knows changing events, if God wills.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00555

There is still another sense of possibility: matter's readiness to receive a new form or quality. This readiness can be stronger or weaker. The nearer the change comes to taking place, and the more of its required conditions are fulfilled, the greater the readiness.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00556

This readiness is not one of the abstract meanings of possibility that exist only in the mind. It arises when certain causes and conditions arise, and it ends when the thing itself comes into being. It is like a shortfall that disappears when something reaches completion, or uncertainty that disappears once the matter is settled. In our philosophy, matter’s readiness for something to come into being stands to it as imperfection stands to completion. This will become clear at the appropriate point, God willing.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00557
This kind of possibility is not a modality. It is treated as a predicate, or as part of a predicate.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00558
Chapter — Another way to understand the concepts that qualify statements
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00559

At first it seems that each of the three concepts—necessity, possibility, and impossibility—could belong to something in three ways: in itself, through another thing, or in relation to another thing. This gives nine combinations. But closer thought rules one out: possibility cannot arise through another thing. It can belong to something in itself or in relation to another. Eight combinations remain. The three cases that hold in themselves—necessity, impossibility, and possibility—form a genuine division that covers every kind of thing and concept as it exists in reality and at its different levels. The exception is a possible essence considered just as it is in itself. At that level, it is not described by possibility, even though possibility is its status in reality. Considered in itself, it is simply what it is.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00560

Still, every kind of denial can be made about an essence at that level, except denying what it is as a concept. This does not settle whether the essence itself exists or whether it is said of something else; those are separate questions. We can say that neither its existence nor its nonexistence is necessary. We can also deny those denials. But there is a great difference between denying something of an essence and saying that the essence has that denial as a feature. The first is a negative statement; the second makes a positive statement about a negation. Possibility, like necessity and impossibility, is said of an essence in the second way, not the first.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00561

If the three-way division is meant to cover a thing in every respect and at every level, including its own essence considered by itself, then it is not exhaustive. An essence may be none of the three at that level. Even if we granted that one of the three belonged to the essence at that level, the essence together with that feature would still belong to it. In that case the essence would no longer be simply itself; it would be itself and the further feature. The three classes would no longer be mutually exclusive and exhaustive.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00562

One of the three categories can belong to a subject at the level of its own essence, as necessity does with God. But that follows from the special nature of that case, not simply from placing it under the general concept. Merely classifying God as necessary does not show that the basis of His necessary existence is His essence itself. Otherwise, after defining each category, we would still need a separate proof that God’s necessity belongs to His essence and is not an added quality or some later consideration.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00563

A concept's being true of something is one matter; the thing's own reality being what makes it true is another. Keep that difference in mind. It will explain why I can later say that a possible essence is never without possibility, however we consider it, without contradicting what I have said here. And know that the concept “necessary in itself” includes several different kinds.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00564

The concept of necessity in itself includes several kinds. First is the Necessary Being: He cannot fail to exist. Nor does His essence have to produce or require existence as though it were an added feature. This is God, who exists through Himself. His necessity is eternal, absolute, and belongs to Him in Himself.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00565

In the second kind, a statement necessarily holds because of what its subject is, although the subject does not cause it to hold. For example, a human being is human, and a human being is an animal. These statements hold necessarily whenever their subject exists. Their necessity is not produced by that existence.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00566

In the third kind, the subject’s own nature is what makes the statement necessary. A triangle, for example, has angles equal to two right angles because it is a triangle. Here the subject’s nature is the reason; its existence is a condition for stating the relationship, not the reason the relationship holds.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00567

Impossibility in itself also has several kinds. One is what cannot exist by its own nature, not because its essence causes or requires its nonexistence. Examples are a second god, absolute nothingness, and pure evil.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00568

Another kind is when a subject cannot have a certain predicate because of what it is, but not because the subject itself causes that predicate’s absence. For example, a human being cannot be an inanimate thing. A third kind is when the subject’s own nature rules out a predicate: four cannot be odd, because what makes four even is exactly what excludes oddness.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00569

Possibility in itself also covers different cases. When something is possible in the strict sense, neither its existence nor its nonexistence is necessary. Both sides can be denied necessity, so we can express the judgment as an affirmation paired with a denial. Consider, too, an imagined whole made of two necessary things, two impossible things, or two opposites. Its existence or nonexistence may be necessary, but not merely because it is a whole. The reason lies in the particular things combined.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00570

The two kinds that hold through something else—necessity and impossibility—apply to everything possible in itself. Neither applies to anything necessary in itself or impossible in itself. We have already seen that what is necessary in itself cannot be necessary through something else.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00571

The three kinds that hold relative to something else do not conflict in reality with the three kinds that hold in themselves, though they differ in meaning. Necessity relative to something else applies to every existing thing, since each thing is either a cause of something else or brought about by something else. A cause and its effect are each necessary relative to the other. Here, “necessary relative to another” means that a thing’s existence is required when considered in relation to something else. This is broader than being caused: the other may demand the thing by its own nature, or the thing may depend on the other for its existence. One of the divine sayings puts it this way: “O Moses, I am what you cannot do without.”
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00572

Impossibility relative to something else applies to every existing thing, whether necessary in itself or possible in itself, when considered alongside the absence of its cause or effect, or of something whose absence would entail the absence of its cause or effect. Likewise, something nonexistent may be impossible or possible relative to another, depending on whether its cause or effect exists.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00573

As for possibility relative to something else, it does not apply to the Necessary, Self-Subsisting Being in relation to any possible thing that exists. It would apply only if we supposed another Necessary Being, or things supposedly made by that other being. It also applies when we compare possible things that both exist, things that both do not exist, or one that exists with one that does not. But in each case, the two must be independent of one another: neither can be the cause or the effect of the other.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00574

This kind of possibility can also apply to things that are impossible in themselves, when they are considered alongside the nonexistence of things that are possible in themselves and what follows from them, provided no connection requires one side or the other.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00575

Clarification. A cause is necessary in relation to its effect because the effect requires that cause to exist. The cause may be necessary in itself, as the First Cause is, or necessary through something else. The effect, in turn, is necessary in relation to its complete cause: when that cause exists in full, the effect cannot fail to exist. For the moment, we are putting aside the fact that the effect receives this necessity from its cause. That is called being necessary through another. Being necessary in relation to another describes a different comparison.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00576

The same distinction applies to two effects of one cause. Each is necessary in relation to the other, because their shared cause requires them both to exist. We are considering each effect in relation to its companion, not yet considering the necessity that belongs to the effect itself. This distinction works at the level of ordinary philosophical analysis. But in our approach, if you follow it, you will discover what needs to be reconsidered. On the ordinary account, the effect is necessary both through its cause and in relation to it. The cause, however, is necessary in relation to its effect, not through its effect. And two effects of one cause are necessary in relation to each other, not through each other.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00577

“Impossible through another” means that another thing makes a thing’s nonexistence necessary. “Impossible in relation to another” means that the other thing, when we compare the two, rules out its existence. Both descriptions apply when we consider the existence of an effect alongside the absence of its cause, or the effect’s absence alongside the presence of its cause. They come apart when those comparisons are reversed—and when we compare the existence of one of two effects from the same cause with the other’s absence, or the absence of one with the other’s existence.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00578

Strict possibility relative to another means that, given the other thing—whether it exists or not—neither the existence nor the nonexistence of the first thing is required. This occurs only between things with no natural causal connection, and no shared cause that produces them both.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00579
Chapter — Why possibility cannot come from something else
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00580

Every thing must be either necessary, possible, or impossible. These three leave no fourth option. First ask whether its existence is necessary. If not, ask whether its nonexistence is necessary. If the answer to both questions is no, it is possible. So our three-part division is really two successive choices, each between a statement and its denial. Every division with more than two parts can be understood in this way. Whatever aspect of a thing we consider, one of the three must apply.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00581

Suppose a thing is possible in itself, whether we consider its essence or one of its features while setting aside the influence of anything else. If it were also possible because of something else, then one and the same thing, in the same respect, would have two possibilities: one from itself and another from something else. This cannot be. Nor can a single possibility come from both the essence and something else at once. We have already seen the same with necessity: if a thing is necessary in itself, it is not necessary because of something else; if it is necessary because of something else, it is not necessary in itself. It is plainly impossible for one thing, in one and the same respect, to have two possibilities.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00582

One thing cannot have two existences, or two nonexistences, in the very same respect. Nor can it have two necessities of existence, two necessities of nonexistence, or two instances of possibility concerning that same existence and nonexistence. These are meanings formed in the mind through their relation to something. They can be multiplied only when the things or aspects they concern are multiplied.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00583

Suppose, then, that a thing’s possibility came from something else. If we set that other thing aside, is the first thing possible in itself? If so, it would have two possibilities in the same respect, which we have ruled out. Or is it necessary to exist or impossible to exist in itself? Then the other thing would have changed what the first thing’s own nature requires, making it the opposite of what it was. That is not what happens when something becomes necessary or impossible because of another while remaining possible in itself. Possibility in itself means that the thing’s nature does not require either existence or nonexistence. It does not mean that its nature requires both necessities to be denied. These are different claims. The first is a simple denial; it does not positively assign a feature of “not being necessary” to the thing. The second does assign a feature to it.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00584

A simple denial does not need the thing’s nature to bring it about. It is enough that the nature itself demands neither existence nor nonexistence. That is why possibility does not follow from an essence in the usual sense of a property produced by that essence. The essence is enough for the statement “it is possible” to be true, but it does not produce possibility.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00585

Some philosophers take possibility to mean that a thing’s nature is equally related to its existence and nonexistence, or that it is true to say that neither is necessary. They treat this as an essential property of the thing. But neither of these is possibility itself. As the argument shows, possibility is a still more basic lack of actuality: pure potential and dependence. The equal relation between existence and nonexistence, when the thing exists or is present in thought, and the truth of positively saying that neither is necessary may follow from the thing’s nature. But they are consequences of possibility, not its true meaning.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00586

Others define possibility as the equal standing of existence and nonexistence in relation to an essence, or as a statement affirming that neither is necessary. They treat it as a property that the essence itself must produce. But how, then, can one side become actual without overturning what the essence requires? Their answer is that the essence considered on its own is not the whole of reality. A feature may be absent at that level but present in reality. The essence, they argue, requires the two sides to be equal when considered by itself, while a cause may still make one side prevail in reality.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00587

But what I have explained shows why this will not do. A possible essence, considered in itself, has no actuality at all. It is pure potential and complete dependence. It has no active power of its own, and it requires nothing until it receives existence from the Necessary, Self-Subsisting One. If it could bring something out of potential and into actuality by itself, then what is only potential, precisely as potential, would help make something actual. Our natural understanding of things rules this out. In itself, an essence that is possible does not require anything—not even the denial of something else.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00588
Clarification and reminder
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00589

Some philosophers take possibility to be a property that necessarily follows from an essence. They then argue that, if possibility came from something else, either two independent causes would produce one effect, or a thing necessary or impossible in itself would become possible in itself. An opponent replies: perhaps each cause acts independently only when the other is absent. If both are present, neither is independent. Think of a whole with several parts. The absence of any one part can account for the whole’s absence; if several parts are missing, their absences do not each act as a separate, complete cause. But this reply cannot establish possibility in itself. On that account, something outside the essence would always matter, whether by being present or absent.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00590

The truth is that the absence of each part causes the whole’s nonexistence only because it occurs alongside what is the real cause of that nonexistence. The real cause is the general fact that at least one necessary part, condition, or other cause is absent. This is one broad, undivided condition, even though the individual absences may be many. The individual absences are not causes in their own right; the shared condition is the cause. A cause of nonexistence may also be less definite than the thing whose nonexistence it explains.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00591

There is no need, then, for the elaborate proposal that the cause of a particular thing’s nonexistence is the nonexistence of that thing’s particular complete cause. Others argue that, if a thing’s possibility came from another, then by itself it would still be allowed to be possible, necessary, or impossible. But if possibility came from another, how could the thing be any of these in itself? They also say that if we imagine the other thing having no effect, the first thing would have to be necessary or impossible in itself, which cannot be.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00592

These arguments lose their force once we understand what possibility in itself means. Consider a thing simply as it is, leaving aside everything else. Neither its existence nor its nonexistence is then necessary. This does not mean its nature produces the absence of necessity. It means we have left out every feature beyond the nature itself, even any denials or relations that might belong to it. Necessity in itself and impossibility in itself must be understood in the same way. These three classes describe the thing viewed on its own.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00593

To clear up a doubt: we have already pointed out that a thing’s being described by a denial at its own level does not mean that its essence itself is the source of that denial. You might say: if we take an essence just as it is, we can deny of it everything that is not part of its essential nature. The denial that existence is necessary is a simple denial, so it can be said of the essence in this way. Then would not possibility in itself be part of the essence, even though we have said it is not?
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00594

The answer turns on where we put the denial. In saying that an essence “is not, considered in itself, anything but itself,” the denial must come before “considered in itself,” so that we deny the claim that the feature belongs to the essence precisely as such. If we instead make “considered in itself” part of the subject—“the essence considered in itself”—and then deny a feature of that subject, the statement may simply be false. Some features cannot in fact be separated from the essence. This distinction makes it possible to answer a puzzle that has troubled many sharp thinkers. If writing can be denied of a human being considered in itself, why can we not also deny that denial, since both writing and not writing are outside the human essence? In the same way, we might deny both necessities of a possible essence and then deny that denial, making it not possible in itself. But we have already shown that no thing is outside the three categories, and that a possible thing remains possible in itself.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00595

The answer is that we must distinguish features that cannot be separated from an essence from those that belong to it only when it exists. An essence considered on its own need not have the second kind of feature—writing or movement, for example—so we may deny those features of it. But some features cannot be separated from an essence even though they are not part of its definition. We may truly describe the essence as having them, without making the essence itself the cause of their presence. Possibility is of this kind. It belongs to an essence before the question of its actual existence arises, so we cannot deny possibility of an essence simply by considering it on its own. This also shows why another reply fails. Some say that an essence can lack possibility when considered on its own, yet still have possibility in reality, just as it can lack writing when considered on its own and acquire writing when it exists. But the comparison is mistaken: possibility does not wait for the essence to exist. Nor is it enough to say that possibility is a simple denial, and that such a denial must therefore be true of the essence on its own. If that were enough, we could just as easily deny possibility itself.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00596

The thing being divided among the three categories is its state in relation to existence and nonexistence. This is a positive state of being described, even if one of its qualifications, such as possibility, is expressed negatively. That is why “this thing is possible” is an affirmative statement whose predicate is negative, not merely the statement “this thing is not necessary.” We affirm of the thing that neither its existence nor its nonexistence is necessary; we do not affirm either necessity. To call something possible is to say truly that this description belongs to it. A careful scholar has made this point.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00597

You may now object: if a thing’s existence depends on another, then its nonexistence depends on that other’s nonexistence, since the absence of a cause brings about the absence of its effect. If a possible thing’s existence is made necessary by another, then the opposite—its existence not being necessary—must also come from another. Likewise, if something is made impossible by another, its nonexistence is necessary; so the opposite, that its nonexistence is not necessary, must also come from another. This would establish possibility through another.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00598

We answer that possibility means being described by the denial of necessity, in the form of an affirmative statement with a negative predicate. It is not the same as a bare denial of necessity, which is a simple negative statement. The opposite of necessary existence is clearly the second kind of statement, not possibility in itself, which is the first.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00599

Nor can we treat the necessity of existence and the necessity of nonexistence as one feature with a single cause. They do not make up a whole whose absence could then be traced to the absence of one cause. They are two distinct and opposing features, each with its own cause, and their causes cannot be present together. Their two opposites therefore do not form one feature with a single cause for its absence—even if we imagine them as one combined whole, let alone as one reality.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00600

Any division must have one clear basis; otherwise, we cannot say what belongs in each part. In The Clear Horizon, this objection is made in another way. If another thing makes existence necessary, the opposite is that existence is not made necessary by another. That, the argument says, is possibility when we consider the thing in itself. The same applies when another thing makes nonexistence necessary. Thus, the objector concludes, there must be possibility through another.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00601

The reply is to look carefully at what the word “another” qualifies. The opposite of “necessity through another” is “not necessary through another”; it is not “a lack of necessity produced by another.” The same distinction applies to impossibility. Nothing prevents necessity produced by another from being absent. What cannot happen is for the absence of necessity itself—possibility—to be produced by another.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00602

Summary and clarification. Some early philosophers treated necessity, possibility, unity, and existence as things added to what exists in the world. Later philosophers said that these are added in the mind, but have no matching forms outside it. We have shown you a balanced way to understand how these concepts can be true and not true of things, and in what sense.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00603

You may hear people who are not engaging the argument seriously dismiss these concepts and say they add nothing to the things described by them, either in the mind or in reality. But our first natural judgment tells us otherwise. When we say that a human being is possibly existent, or that a heavenly sphere is possibly existent, “possibility” does not mean “human being” in the first case and “sphere” in the second. It is one meaning that applies to both. If “possibility” meant human nature when said of a human being, and the nature of a sphere when said of a sphere, the word would name two different things. It would add no shared meaning beyond “human being” and “sphere.” If it meant the same thing as “human being” and “sphere” in both cases, then those two things would have the same meaning, which is plainly false.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00604

So when “possibility” is said of different essences, it is not identical with any one of them. It is another, shared feature that applies to them all. One philosopher was astonished that these thinkers agree with defenders of the truth when they argue that the world needs a Creator because it is possible and depends on a cause, yet, when discussing possibility, say that it is nothing more than the thing itself. It is as if they were saying: “The world needs a Creator because the world is the world.”
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00605

A principle of the Illuminationist school. Suhrawardī offers a rule for understanding why possibility and similar concepts exist in the mind without having separate forms in the world. Suppose a general concept had a separate form outside the mind. If that required the same concept to be applied again and again, a series would arise with no end. If existence were a thing added to an existing essence, that added existence would itself have to exist. Its existence would then need another existence, and so on without end. What is more, the whole chain would itself need to exist, starting a second endless chain. The same reasoning would repeat. Yet the first existence could not be established unless all these chains were already established.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00606

The same difficulty arises with unity. An essence and its added unity would each need unity; existence would need unity, and unity would need existence. Their combinations would generate further endless series. Possibility would have to exist, the existence of possibility would itself be possible, and new series would arise. If that existence were necessary, possibility would no longer be something added to a thing. And still more series would form between possibility and necessity through another, between existence and necessity, and between unity and necessity. So concepts that would produce these endlessly multiplying chains cannot have separate forms outside the mind. They are ideas drawn from things. They do not correspond to extra objects added to essences in the world, nor do they reach a final, fixed point at which the mind can stop repeating them.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00607
Discussion and clarification
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00608

There are several reasons to doubt this rule. First, its defenders themselves say that the Necessary Being is nothing but existence and necessity: He exists through Himself and is necessary in Himself. They do not deny that He exists outside the mind. Yet their account of existence contradicts this. They say that existence is only an idea in the mind, with no form in the world, yet they also say that God’s essence is the source of all forms and the root of all realities.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00609

Second, the person who introduced and defended this rule admits that one and the same meaning can exist in different ways. Sometimes it is a feature of something else; sometimes it is a reality in its own right. It can be stronger or weaker, more or less complete. Why not allow the same for existence and unity, as we argued earlier? Each can have different ways of being real, from the most complete to the least complete. At its highest level, each is one reality that depends on nothing else and is necessary in itself. At its lowest, it is only an idea in the mind or a relation, with nothing independently real corresponding to it.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00610

The natures of things have no reality on their own; they are real only through existence. But existence does not need something else to make it real. It is what makes those natures real. How, then, could existence have no reality? Its reality is itself. Existence does not need a second existence to make it exist. Otherwise we would have to go on adding existences. The mind can imagine a further existence for it, just as it can imagine a further light for light. But light makes things visible, and is itself visible without the help of a second light. Otherwise we would need light after light without end. Yet the mind can imagine a light for light, then another light for that light, and so on, until it stops making these mental distinctions.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00611

The same applies to unity. It is a feature of things in the world because it is existence itself in reality, though different from existence in meaning. Often something has a reality and essence beyond its meaning and beyond the form it takes in the mind, as existence and its perfect qualities do. Sometimes a thing has only a meaning and no reality in the world, as with possibility, impossibility, the joining of opposites, a partner to God, and similar ideas. The same is true of negations and relations. Sometimes several meanings exist through one existence and are one with a single reality. Knowledge, power, and life, for example, are one with the existence of God, may He be exalted.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00612

This also answers an argument that a respected philosopher gives in Discussions. He calls it strong and convincing: “We can meet those who say that being existent is existence itself halfway. We say that existence and unity are alike: according to you, both must exist in the world; according to us, both are only ideas in the mind. Suppose you reject an endless chain in the case of existence by saying that existence is the state of being existent. Still, existence and unity have different meanings, and we can understand one without the other. Unity cannot simply mean existence, nor existence unity. So if existence exists, it has unity; and if unity exists, it has existence, which in turn has another unity, existing through another existence, and so on. An endless chain of existence and unity must follow. It is no answer to say that the unity of existence is existence itself, or that the existence of unity is unity itself. The meanings of existence and unity differ, and two distinct things cannot be one and the same thing in themselves.”
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00613

That is the heart of his argument. He assumes that two different meanings cannot come from one and the same reality. But he has not proved it. One reality, even considered in the same respect, can answer to several different descriptions. Zayd’s existence, for example, can be caused, known, provided for, and dependent. The difference among these meanings does not require each to have a separate existence. The same is true of the divine qualities, which all philosophers agree are one with God’s single existence. In short, different meanings alone do not prove that the reality or way of existing for each must differ. A further argument is needed to show that their underlying realities differ.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00614

This is also supported by what Avicenna says in The Healing, in the section on divine things. The fact that something understands and is understood does not mean that its essence, or even our way of thinking about it, is two things. Nor does the fact that something in motion requires a mover mean that this requirement itself must be a separate thing, or the very thing it requires. A different line of inquiry is needed to show that what moves cannot be what moves it. For this reason, some people could imagine that there is something that moves itself until proof showed that this is impossible. The ideas “mover” and “moved” alone do not prove it. Likewise, two related things are known to be two because of something beyond the relation imagined by the mind. That is the end of Avicenna’s statement.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00615

I say: Avicenna’s point is that two ideas can differ without proving that the things they describe are either one or two. We need a separate argument to decide whether the realities behind them are the same or different. “Moving” differs in meaning from “being moved,” just as “parent” differs from “child,” and “understanding” from “being understood.” But reason shows that, when no matter is involved, the one who understands and what is understood are one in reality, despite the difference between the two ideas. A mover and what it moves, by contrast, really are different. The same is true of the two sides of a relation. So understand this carefully: people have gone astray on this point.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00616

The weakness of this rule is now clear in some cases, such as unity and existence. Showing that these have no reality in the world does not prove that other concepts lack it. Another argument is needed to show that those other concepts are only ideas in the mind. We have already pointed out how these meanings attach to realities and essences. Consider the matter carefully and reflect deeply.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00617

You have learned that possibility describes an essence when we consider the essence just as it is, without considering its relation to a complete cause. What describes an essence considered in that way cannot be an actual feature in the world; it must be an idea in the mind. Also, possibility has a negative meaning. Negations, as negations, have no share in existence, whether in the world or in the mind.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00618

Consider the First Effect. It shows why those who treat possibility as a real feature added to a thing’s nature are mistaken. They themselves say that the First Effect is possible in itself. They also regard it as beginning in its own being, so it must first be possible and only then exist. For something to gain existence through another, it must first be possible in itself. But if its possibility comes first, that possibility must itself be possible. It cannot be necessary in itself, since it depends on something else; nor can there be two beings necessary in themselves. So this possibility, too, would need a cause to bring it about.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00619

If that cause were the Necessary Being, two impossible results would follow. First, one source would bring about both the First Effect and its possibility. But for one source to produce two things, it must act in two different ways. That cannot be true of the absolutely one divine reality.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00620

Second, possibility would itself be produced by an agent outside the thing it describes. But we have already shown that a thing’s possibility cannot be produced by a cause—least of all by something other than the thing’s own nature.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00621

They cannot escape this by saying that possibility does not come before the First Effect and the other eternal beings. That would mean possibility only comes about after the thing exists. Yet they admit that possible things begin in their own being. Their possibility must therefore come before the necessity they receive from another, since necessity through another depends on a thing first being possible in itself. What belongs to a thing through itself comes before what belongs to it through another, especially when what it receives through another depends on what belongs to it through itself.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00622

Nor does it help to say that possibility has one meaning for eternal beings and another for other things. Real possibility—the opposite of necessity and impossibility—applies to every effect. If the beings that exist eternally through divine creation were not possible in themselves in this sense, they would be necessary in themselves or impossible in themselves. They are neither.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00623

Nor does it help to appeal to a note found among Avicenna’s drafts, called Fairness and Redress, which says that the generosity of the First Truth does not allow possibility to come before the effects it creates. The question is not which came first in time. We are not claiming that possibility comes before things that begin in time but not before things created without a beginning in time. We are asking what comes first by its very nature. If possibility were an actual feature in the world, and existence through another required possibility in itself, then possibility would come first. What a thing has through itself comes before what it has through another. Those who say that possibility exists in the world have no way out of this difficulty unless they accept the account we have established: possibility and similar concepts exist through something else but have no existence in themselves.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00624

If possibility had its own actual form in the world, even as an attribute attached to something else, it would not be a feature that belongs to an essence considered apart from existence and nonexistence. A feature that belongs to an essence in itself—whether the words are used in their strict sense or more broadly—must be an idea in the mind. If possibility had an actual form, existence through another could not attach to an essence. For if the lack of necessity for existence and nonexistence were an actual feature, it would attach to an essence that exists and conflict with the necessity that is also an actual feature. But if possibility describes an essence considered in itself, without regard to the source of its existence or nonexistence, then there is no conflict when existence or nonexistence comes to it from elsewhere. The two descriptions concern different subjects: the essence considered in itself, and the essence as it exists through another.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00625

It is also mistaken to define a possible thing by saying that its own nature makes neither its existence nor its nonexistence necessary. When we divide things into necessary, possible, and impossible, we consider how each stands in relation to existence itself. We do not restrict the meaning of existence or compare the thing with anything else.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00626
Objections and replies
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00627

Those who say that possibility and similar ideas—necessity, existence, thinghood, and unity—have real forms in the world, additional to the essence of the possible, necessary, existent, thing, or one, offer several arguments for their view.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00628

Their first argument is this: we distinguish a thing that can exist in the world from one that can exist only in the mind. They say the difference must be that the first has possibility in the world, while the second has possibility only in the mind. They argue in the same way about the other descriptions.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00629

Second, they say, a thing must be either necessary, possible, or impossible. So if its possibility were not real in the world, it would have to be necessary or impossible there. If its existence were not real, it would not exist; if its oneness were not real, it would be many. These conclusions would contradict our judgments that things in the world can be possible, existent, and one.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00630

Third, if these were only mental ideas and descriptions, not realities in the things themselves, the mind could attach them to any essence it chose. Then every concept, even impossible ones such as a partner to God, the joining of opposites, and absolute nothingness, would be possible. The same reasoning would apply to the other ideas.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00631

Fourth, an event must be preceded by possibility. An agent brings it about only because it is possible in the world, not merely possible in the mind. Otherwise it would exist only in the mind. So whatever exists in the world must have a possibility in the world before it exists.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00632

These are the strongest arguments for saying that possibility and other mental ideas of this kind have actual forms in the world. But someone seeking the truth can answer them. What is agreed is that possibility and similar ideas are additional to the essences to which the mind relates them. When the mind considers, for example, the essence of a human being, it finds that possibility is neither that essence nor part of it. The same is true of other descriptions that are neither the essence nor one of its parts. But it does not follow that these additional ideas have forms in the world. The only exception is the description that is existence, and also individual unity, which, for those firmly grounded in knowledge, is existence itself. That claim rests on a special proof about existence.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00633

None of these arguments proves that existence has a real form in the world. We came to that conclusion through a gift of unseen knowledge, support from the spiritual realm, aid from above, and heavenly grace. Nor does saying that something is “possible in the world” or “existent in the world” prove that its possibility or existence is itself in the world. We have already seen that a dependent existence—the existence a thing has through something else—can differ from existence in itself. The mind judges that a possible thing is possible in the world, as explained earlier; it also judges that it is possible in the mind. Possibility is therefore a mental feature: its own particular way of existing is in the mind. The mind may relate it to something in the world, or to something in the mind, or may judge without qualification that it applies equally to both.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00634

No one can claim that, if impossibility has no form in the world, an impossible thing is not impossible there; or that, unless impossibility itself exists in the world, the thing must be either necessary or possible. The same answer applies to the second argument. Impossibility, necessity, and possibility are alike in this respect: they are ideas in the mind, with no separate forms in the world, even though things in the world and in the mind can be described by them.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00635

In The Paths of Discussion, Suhrawardi says that possibility, necessity, impossibility, and existence have no separate reality in things. He compares them with the ideas studied in logic: whether something is general or individual, whether a feature belongs to its nature or happens to accompany it, and whether an idea names a broader kind or what distinguishes one kind from another. These are ways the mind describes things; they are not separate objects inside those things. A particular person can be individual, and “human being” can be universal, even though universality and individuality themselves cannot exist as separate things in the world. In the same way, a thing can be described as possible or impossible even though these descriptions have no separate forms there.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00636

But the comparison is not quite right. Possibility and impossibility do not work in exactly the same way as being general or individual. The descriptions used in logic depend on how a thing exists in the mind. The descriptions we are discussing here can sometimes depend on what a thing is like in the world. In both cases, the descriptions themselves exist only in thought.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00637

As for the fourth argument, which concerns possibility in particular, it depends on what “possibility” means. If it means that something is ready to come into existence—that the conditions now allow it to receive existence from the cause that brings it about—then we can accept, for now, that every event beginning in time has this kind of possibility in the world before it occurs. We will explain later what it means to call this an actual thing in the world.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00638

But if “possibility” means the state of an essence considered in itself, we agree only that this possibility comes before existence as an idea and a way of considering the essence. Even if a thing had no earlier period of nonexistence in time, the mind can consider it as not yet existing. We also say that not every event can have an actual possibility in the world before it exists.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00639

There is no end to the events still to come. One event will follow another without limit, as religious teachings and philosophical arguments affirm. Examples include the movements of the people of Paradise and the punishments of the people of Hell. If each event, or each event still to come, had its own possibility in the world, matter would contain an unlimited number of possibilities. If some events had no possibility, then some would occur without a prior possibility, and by the argument just given they would have to be necessary or impossible.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00640

Some may accept an unlimited series of possibilities and say that they are not ordered one after another: each event has its own possibility, and all these possibilities exist together. We will show that such a collection cannot exist, for two reasons.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00641

First, possibility has one meaning. A thing, considered simply as possible, does not differ from another possible thing because of possibility itself. Nor can the differences come from prime matter, which holds these possibilities, because matter is pure potential and has no distinctions of its own, as we will explain. So possibilities in themselves could differ only because the things they are possibilities of differ. But these are events that do not yet exist, in an unlimited series. A thing cannot be distinguished from another by being related to something that does not exist: what has no reality cannot distinguish one thing from another.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00642

You might reply that we can think about infinitely many future things and so distinguish the possibilities attached to them. But we cannot hold infinitely many separate things in the mind at once, each with its own details. We may have a general idea of an unlimited number, but that is different from holding an unlimited number of distinct things in the mind. If we think only of possibilities and future things in general, every possibility has the same relation to every future thing. One possibility is no more distinct from another than one future thing is from another.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00643

Second, even if we grant this account, it in effect accepts our point. Where possibilities become distinct is also where they become real. If the mind alone distinguishes them, then they have this distinct existence only in the mind. If we suppose instead that their difference lies in the world, then our understanding of that difference must follow the difference already there. But the proposed account says that the mind’s own imagining makes them different. It would then make the thing depend on itself, which is impossible.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00644

Here is the second reason. Suppose matter, which carries an unlimited number of possibilities, were divided into two halves. Then one of three things must be true: each half keeps the very same unlimited possibilities that the whole had; each half gains a new unlimited set of possibilities at the moment of division; or each half contains only a limited number. None of these outcomes is possible.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00645
The first outcome would mean that one and the same thing existed at the same time in two different places, which is impossible.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00646

The second outcome would mean that new possibilities appeared in each half. But because these possibilities are themselves new events, each would need an earlier possibility. If those earlier possibilities were new too, they would in turn need still earlier possibilities. At the moment of division, no agent could produce even the first layer unless endlessly many earlier layers had already come about. But nothing can happen at one moment if it requires an endless succession to have happened first. This would also mean that the events whose possibilities had just arisen were impossible before those possibilities appeared, even though the argument says that anything without an actual possibility must be impossible. Things would shift from being impossible in themselves to being possible in themselves.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00647

The third outcome would leave each half with a limited number of possibilities. But two limited numbers add up to a limited number. The total number of possibilities in one body would then be limited, while the events they belong to are unlimited. Nor can we say that each half contains an unlimited set that is not new, each set being half of the unlimited set in the whole. A body can always be divided again. Each new cut brings back the same problem. Since we have supposed that the possibilities do not arise at the moment of division, they must have occupied distinct places before the division. They cannot move from one place to another. So, after the division, some would remain in one half and the rest in the other.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00648

If infinitely many possibilities already occupied different places, then the body would contain infinitely many distinct parts, distinguished by the features—the possibilities—that belong to them. This would mean either that it is made of indivisible parts, which is impossible, or that it contains an unlimited number of parts of measurable size, making the whole body unlimited in size. That too is impossible, as we will prove later. How could a body with a fixed size contain endlessly many separate places, each with its own feature? And since each part can be divided again, the same problem returns inside every part.
